The Revenge Game: Do Players Beat Their Former Teams?

A player-stint fixed-effects study of NFL skill players facing franchises they used to play for (1,547 games in the main sample, 2001 to 2025, from data covering 1999 to 2025), with a larger NBA companion study (2002-03 to 2022-23). Version 0.4, the final revision after three referee and editorial review cycles. Every number below is read from ebk-revenge-game/outputs/tables.

Summary of findings

1. In the NFL there is a small positive revenge-game effect. Against a franchise he played 8 or more games for, a skill player scores +0.35 PPR fantasy points (fpts from here on) more than in his other games that season, after adjusting for the opponent's defense against his position, home field, the Vegas implied team total and division games (95% player-cluster bootstrap CI [+0.03, +0.68], cluster-robust p=0.027, n=1,547 games, 620 players). That is 4.6% of an average game and 0.06 standard deviations of a player's game-to-game swing.

2. It clears the tests for chance, but it is imprecise, and we cannot tell where in the distribution it comes from. A permutation test that compares the real t-statistic with 1,000 fake former teams gives p=0.029; 12 of 14 specifications have intervals above zero, with point estimates from +0.18 to +0.72. Removing the 10 largest of 1,547 revenge games moves the estimate to +0.20 (p=0.191), but removing the 10 largest of any 1,547 games does the same: when random ordinary games of the same players are all given the same lift, dropping their 10 biggest moves b by −0.158 on average (200 simulations), against −0.155 for the real revenge games. Fantasy scores are right-skewed, so this check measures precision, not where the effect lives. Quantile and boom/bust comparisons show no heavier right tail; if anything revenge games have fewer duds (Robustness, Mechanism).

3. The pre-kickoff baseline understates it. Comparing each game only with the player's earlier games that season gives +0.18. On nearly the same games (1,121 of 1,131; singleton stints drop), the stint fixed-effects estimate is +0.49, and a later-games baseline gives +0.59. Stints that contain a revenge game tend to fade within the season (−0.035 fpts per game of the stint, CI [−0.078, +0.007], versus +0.032 for other stints). With a stint-specific linear trend the effect is +0.43 (p=0.009). The same kickoff comparison restricted to players who had changed teams, so revenge games are compared with games of the same kind of player under the same forecast rule, gives +0.39 (SE 0.19, p=0.045): the revenge increment a manager could have used at kickoff is about +0.35 to +0.43.

4. It may not be about revenge, but the placebo evidence is narrower than it first looks. The NFL future-team placebo is flat when pooled (+0.02); a timing split made after seeing the data shows +0.46 in the season before a player joins (p=0.082, interval [−0.09, +1.00]). In the NBA the placebo is +0.14 points and decays with distance from the move, as revenge does. The within player-by-franchise design gives −0.03 (SE 0.10), but it identifies only from players who faced a franchise before joining it: 7,072 of 13,559 NBA revenge games, none against the player's first franchise. Revenge games against the first franchise (45% of the total) run +0.35 against +0.18 for later franchises (difference p=0.081) and cannot be tested this way. An audition effect (teams acquire players who just played well against them) explains the placebo but does not by itself inflate revenge games, which come after the move; revenge games are contaminated only if a lasting player-by-franchise edge exists that teams also select on. The NBA venue pattern cuts against that: the placebo is flat by venue (+0.13 home, +0.14 away) while revenge is +0.13 at home and +0.38 at the old arena (Wald p=0.016, q=0.08 across five NBA dimensions). The NFL pair design is uninformative (+0.13, SE 0.44).

5. No subgroup is reliably different. Across 28 subgroups no coefficient survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction (smallest q=0.14). Level heterogeneity is specification-sensitive: classified on the previous season (a pre-determined measure), players at 8-14 fpts per game show +0.88 and depth players +0.01 (Wald p=0.038, q=0.38); v01 classified on a stint mean that contained the game and found no pattern (Heterogeneity).

6. Fantasy answer: the revenge bump is the size of a home game (+0.31) or a one-standard-deviation softer matchup (+0.39), 29% of the softest-vs-toughest matchup gap (+1.20), and 6% of one standard deviation of game-to-game noise (5.87 fpts). For players who scored 10+ fpts per game the previous season it is +0.72 (CI [+0.04, +1.37]), but that is the same exploratory level dimension as the Heterogeneity section: the 10+ versus under-10 difference is +0.55 (p=0.137), so starters are not reliably different from everyone else and the pooled estimate is the better forecast. A tiebreaker, never a reason to start a worse player.

Abbreviations. fpts = PPR fantasy points. FE = fixed effects. DvP = opponent defense vs position (Method). CI = 95% player-cluster bootstrap interval (1,000 draws unless stated). q = Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value. Plain-language definitions are in the glossary below.

Glossary

Every statistical term used in this report, in one line each.

TermMeaning
p-valuehow often a result at least this large would appear by chance if the true effect were zero; small means surprising under 'no effect'
95% CI (interval)the range of effects consistent with the data; here the middle 95% of 1,000 bootstrap re-estimates
SD (standard deviation)the typical size of a deviation from the average
SE (standard error)the SD of an estimate across hypothetical repeat samples; roughly, its uncertainty
Residualwhat is left after the model's prediction: actual minus expected
Fixed effect (stint FE)a separate baseline for every player-season-team, so comparisons are within the same player's season
Leave-one-outan average computed without the game in question, so a game never helps set its own expectation
DvPhow many fpts a defense allowed to a position relative to those players' own averages, excluding the current game
q-valuea p-value adjusted for testing many subgroups at once (Benjamini-Hochberg)
pppercentage points: the difference between two percentages
Wald testa test of whether several subgroup effects are equal to each other
Permutation testre-running the analysis on fake former teams to see how often a result this strong appears by chance
t-statistican estimate divided by its standard error; comparable across samples of different size

Question & data

The question: when a player faces a franchise he used to play for, does he produce more than he would have in an ordinary game with the same matchup? "More" is measured against the player's own level that season, not against league averages, because the population of players who get to face a former team is not a random one (Limitations).

The sources below are all public and cached locally. The NFL weekly file has a row only when a player records a stat, which is why the snap-count file is used for a robustness check (Robustness).

After keeping QB/RB/WR/TE rows from regular-season and playoff games, the NFL file has 156,949 player-game rows (of 476,159 rows for all positions); 1 duplicate player-game row is dropped when careers are walked, leaving the 156,948 in the funnel (Cohort). Franchise codes are canonicalized so a relocated team is one franchise (OAK = LV, SD = LAC, STL = LA). The NBA files have 739,524 rows before filters; ESPN team ids already follow the franchise through relocations (Seattle to Oklahoma City, New Jersey to Brooklyn). The NBA archive ends with 2022-23, and that season's file stops a few games short for every team; the missing games are dropped, not imputed.

Cohort construction

Each player's career is walked in date order. For every game we record how many games he had already played for the opponent franchise. Every term used below is defined here.

TermDefinition
Revenge game (main)opponent is a franchise he recorded 8+ games for (about half a season), and is not his current team. The count includes playoff games and only games with a stat line, so it can fall a game short of the official record when he played without recording a stat (Andre Johnson: 172 here, 173 officially)
Minor former teamopponent is a franchise he recorded 1-7 games for; kept as its own dummy, never in the comparison group
Future team (placebo)opponent is a franchise he has not played for yet but later records 8+ games for
Meeting number1 = first game he played vs that franchise since his last game for it
Seasons sinceseason of this game minus his last season with the opponent (0 = midseason move)
Left by tradetrades.csv shows the opponent trading him away between his first game there and this game (ledger starts in 2002)
Full careerrookie season 1999 or later, so his entire franchise history is inside the data
Stintplayer × season × team; a midseason trade starts a new stint
Level coming inhis fpts per game in his most recent earlier season (all teams, regular season); used for level subgroups (v02)

Method, step by step

Outcome

fpts are nflverse PPR fantasy points: 1×rec + 0.1×(rec yds + rush yds) + 6×(rec TD + rush TD) + 0.04×pass yds + 4×pass TD − 2×INT − 2×fumbles lost + 2×2-pt. Position-specific raw stats (yards, TDs, targets, carries) are analyzed with the same model in the Mechanism section.

The player's own level

In plain English: a game is judged against the same player's other games that season. For player i in stint s with ns regular-season games, the leave-one-out mean for game g is LOOig = (Σh∈s fptsih − fptsig) / (ns − 1), and the raw residual is rig = fptsig − LOOig. Only stints with ns ≥ 4 are used.

Opponent defense vs position (DvP)

In plain English: how much a defense helped or hurt players at his position that season, compared with their own averages. For defense d, season t and position k: DvPdtk,−g = Σ rjh / N over every other player-game (j,h) at position k against d in season t, excluding all rows from game g itself. It is in fpts per player-game: positive means players beat their own averages against that defense. Its standard deviation is 1.20 fpts. Because DvP is itself a noisy average, its coefficient is attenuated toward zero, so the matchup comparisons in the Fantasy calibration section understate matchup relative to revenge (conservative for the fantasy conclusion).

Game context

Vegas implied points for the player's team: (total + spread)/2 at home and (total − spread)/2 away, where nflverse's spread_line is the expected home margin. Home = 1 for a true home game; neutral-site games get their own dummy. Division = 1 if the teams share a division.

Main model

In plain English: every player-season gets its own baseline, so the revenge term can only pick up how a revenge game differs from that same player's other games that year, after the matchup, venue and Vegas adjustments.

fptsig = αs(i,g) + β·Revengeig + βm·Minorig + βf·Futureig + γ1DvPig + γ2Homeig + γ3Neutralig + γ4Impliedig + γ5Divig + εig

Fitted values are written in Latin letters: b is the estimate of β, a of α, g of γ. αs is one intercept per stint. Estimation is by the within transformation: every variable has its stint mean subtracted (ỹ = y − ȳs), then OLS on the demeaned data gives b = (X̃'X̃)−1X̃'ỹ. Singleton stints are dropped.

Uncertainty

Why cluster by player: a player's games are linked (a good player is good every week), so 17 games from one player are not 17 independent pieces of evidence. Why bootstrap: rebuild the dataset 1,000 times by drawing players at random (some twice, some not at all), re-fit each time, and report the middle 95% of the 1,000 answers.

Standard errors are cluster-robust by player (Liang-Zeger CR1): V = c·(X̃'X̃)−1 [Σc (X̃c'ûc)(X̃c'ûc)'] (X̃'X̃)−1 with c = G/(G−1) · (N−1)/(N−K), where G = players, N = games and K = regressors. Stint fixed effects are nested within players, so they are not subtracted in the small-sample factor (the reghdfe and Cameron-Miller convention; v01 subtracted them, which inflated every SE by about 5%). Fixed effects that are not nested in players, such as opponent-season effects, are subtracted. p-values use a t distribution with G−1 degrees of freedom. The reported 95% intervals come from a pairs cluster bootstrap: resample 2,692 players with replacement 1,000 times. Because stints are nested within players, the demeaned data do not change when whole players are resampled, so each draw is βb = (Σc wcX̃c'X̃c)−1(Σc wcX̃c'ỹc) with multinomial weights w. With the corrected degrees of freedom the analytic SE of the main coefficient (0.160) matches the bootstrap SE (0.161).

The bootstrap interval and the cluster-robust p-value are two ways of measuring the same uncertainty, and at the margin they can disagree (a p-value just above 0.05 with an interval that just excludes zero). Where they do, charts color by the bootstrap interval and tables report both.

Multiple comparisons

Why this matters: test 28 groups and one or two will look "significant" by luck. Benjamini-Hochberg raises each p-value to account for how many tests were run; the adjusted value is q, and q < 0.05 is the bar. Subgroup coefficients (Heterogeneity) are one family of 28 tests: sort p ascending, q(k) = minj≥k p(j)·m/j. The four distribution-shape outcomes (Mechanism) are a separate family of four.

Matched comparison

As a model-light check, each revenge game is compared with the k=3 games from the same stint and the same venue (home or away) against never-connected opponents with the closest DvP. The effect is the mean of fptsrevenge − mean(fptsmatched), with a player-cluster bootstrap CI.

Placebos

(a) Future-team games: same model, the Future dummy; in v02 also split by seasons until he joins. (b) Fake former teams: for each of the players with a real revenge game, a random franchise he never played for is drawn, and games against it after he left his first team are flagged; bfake and its t-statistic are estimated with the real terms kept in the model. Repeated 1,000 times. Each draw uses the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell shortcut, which gives exactly the same coefficient as re-running the full regression and makes 1,000 re-runs fast: residualize the demeaned fake dummy and demeaned fpts on the other regressors, then bfake = Σx̃ỹ / Σx̃2, with an exact cluster-robust SE. The permutation p-value compares t-statistics (v02), because the fake draws contain fewer games than the real test (Placebo tests). (c) Within player-by-franchise: stint FE plus a fixed effect for every player × opponent-franchise pair (Placebo tests, NBA replication).

Why the pre-game baseline (S11) is low

S11 compares each game with the average of the player's earlier games that season, which is what a fantasy manager knew at kickoff. It gives +0.18. On nearly the same games (1,121 of 1,131; singleton stints drop), the stint fixed-effects model gives +0.49 (S11-FE), so the drop is caused by the baseline, not by the sample. The reason is in-season drift: stints that contain a revenge game slope −0.035 fpts per game (CI [−0.078, +0.007]), other stints +0.032 (CI [+0.015, +0.050]). A player who is fading looks worse against his own earlier games and better against his later ones, so a prior-games baseline is biased down and a later-games baseline (S11-future, +0.59) is biased up. Giving every stint its own linear trend (S13) gives +0.43 (p=0.009). A second, smaller reason: S11 cannot use revenge games in the first three games of a stint, and those show +0.10 against +0.44 later (difference −0.34, p=0.261; not significant). S11 compares moved players' revenge games with everyone's forecast errors, and players still on their first team drift up. Restricting the comparison to players who had changed teams keeps the kickoff forecast rule but compares like with like: +0.39 (95% CI [+0.01, +0.77], p=0.045, 1,131 revenge games), and +0.39 with a game-order control. The +0.18 is best read as the revenge effect minus the moved-player fade, which affects every game he plays, not just the revenge game. For a start/sit decision the revenge increment at kickoff is about +0.39.

Removing the 10 biggest of 1,547 revenge games halves the estimate and removing the 10 worst raises it. That pattern does not show the effect lives in the tail, because fpts are right-skewed: the 10 largest of any 1,547 games sit far above the mean. The benchmark gives randomly chosen ordinary games of the same players (the same number per player as their real revenge games) a uniform lift equal to the real b, then applies the same drops, 200 times:

A small lift for every game produces the same drop-the-top-10 result as the real data, so the check measures precision (10 games' worth of outcomes can move the estimate by half, which the interval [+0.03, +0.68] already says), not where the effect lives. Placebo tests

Two placebos ask whether the method finds "revenge" where there can be none. The future-team placebo uses games against a franchise the player will join later (the "audition" game). The fake-former-team permutation replaces the real former team with a random team he never played for, 1,000 times. The estimates:

TestEstimateIntervalpGamesNote
Real revenge coefficient (main model)+0.354[+0.029, +0.683]0.0271,547
Future-team placebo (before he joins them)+0.016[−0.247, +0.263]0.9002,921no revenge motive possible
Fake former team: mean of 1,000 permutation draws−0.006[−0.386, +0.367]n/a882lo/hi = 2.5/97.5 percentiles of the draws
Fake former teams rescaled to the real sample's precision (t x real SE)−0.008[−0.332, +0.294]n/a1,547what fake teams produce with as many games as the real test

The fake draws involve fewer games than the real test (about 882 per draw versus 1,547), so raw fake coefficients are noisier than the real estimate. Comparing raw coefficients (the v01 method) therefore overstates the p-value; comparing t-statistics puts both on the same footing. The diagnostics:

Permutation diagnosticValueNote
Permutation p-value (studentized): share of fake draws with |t| >= |real t|0.029two-sided; compares like with like (v02 headline)
Permutation p-value (raw b, v01): share of fake draws with |b| >= |real b|0.080conservative: fakes average far fewer games than the real test
SD of fake t-statistics0.994should be close to 1 if SEs are honest
False-positive rate: share of fake draws with p < 0.050.050should be close to 0.05 if SEs are honest

The studentized permutation p-value is 0.029, in line with the cluster-robust p=0.027. The fake t-statistics have SD 0.99 and 5.0% of fake draws reach p<0.05, so the standard errors are honest. (Each player has only about twenty eligible fake franchises, so draws are not fully independent and the false-positive rate carries somewhat more Monte Carlo error than a binomial on 1,000 draws.) The distribution:

Histogram: t-statistics for 1,000 fake former teams. Solid red: the real revenge t-statistic. Dotted: its mirror image (two-sided test).

So the NBA −0.03 means: for players who had faced a franchise before joining it, games after leaving are no better than games before joining. It says nothing about returns to the first franchise, which are about half the NBA revenge games (6,066 of the 6,487 non-identifying games) and carry the larger estimate. The same holds in the NFL (986 of 1,170 non-identifying games are against the first franchise). The groups also differ in career stage, so the split is descriptive, not causal.

What the placebo evidence does and does not show. A pure audition effect (teams acquire players who just played well against them) raises the pre-join games and explains the placebo, but it does nothing to games after the move; under that story revenge games are clean and the within-pair design is biased against revenge. Revenge games are contaminated only if a lasting player-by-franchise component exists (scheme fit, familiarity) that teams also select on. The NBA placebo two or more seasons before joining (+0.12) is hard to square with auditions and fits a lasting component. The NBA venue pattern cuts the other way (NBA replication): the placebo shows no venue gap, while revenge does. The NFL season-before bump comes from a timing split made after seeing the data, and its interval includes zero.

It also depends heavily on how "level" is measured. v01 classified players by their stint mean, which includes the revenge game itself, so a big revenge game can promote a player into a higher tier. Excluding connected games from the stint mean biases it the other way (a big revenge game can no longer count, and regression to the mean pushes the other way). Only the previous season is set before the game. The three versions:

Under the pre-determined measure, established contributors (8-14 fpts per game last season) show the largest estimate and depth players show none; under the two stint-based measures the pattern is different or reversed. We report the pre-determined version and treat the level pattern as exploratory. Two other results cut against the narrative: the first meeting after leaving (+0.20) is not larger than later meetings (+0.56, Wald p=0.219), and players who were stars for the old team (14+ fpts per game there) show +0.14 with a wide interval.

Fantasy calibration and the famous games

To judge whether +0.35 fpts matters for a lineup decision, it helps to put it next to the other game-level factors that fantasy managers already use, all estimated in the same model.

The chart makes the comparison visual. The revenge bump is about the size of a home game or a one-standard-deviation softer defense, has the widest interval of the group, and is a small fraction of the ordinary game-to-game swing. Because DvP is measured with noise, the matchup rows are if anything understated.

The games people remember

An objective "marquee" set: first meeting after leaving, 32+ games with the old team, and 14+ fpts per game while there (a real star for them). There are 77 such games in the main sample. They average +0.06 fpts versus the model's expectation (player-cluster bootstrap CI [−1.55, +1.65]; median −1.16), and 41.6% beat it. With 77 games this cannot distinguish zero from the overall +0.35. The full list is in nfl_marquee_games.csv. Expectations are leave-one-out in v02: a game's own result no longer enters its expectation.

That gap between a remembered list and the objective marquee set is itself the best illustration of why the revenge game feels real. The revenge effect on points is +0.26 (CI [+0.16, +0.37]), about 2.6% of an average game. Minutes rise by +0.26, but points per 36 minutes also rise (+0.29, CI [+0.15, +0.43]), so it is not only playing time. The important caveat is the placebo: +0.14 points against a team the player will later join, clearly above zero. Revenge minus placebo = +0.12 (p=0.066, CI [0.00, +0.26]), and the within player-by-franchise design gives −0.03 (95% CI [−0.24, +0.17], 1,137 identifying pairs). Both approaches assume the player-franchise component is the same before joining and after leaving; the within-pair design imposes it pair by pair, which removes differences in which players make up each group. It covers only the 7,072 revenge games in pairs where the player faced the franchise before joining it, none of them against his first franchise (Placebo tests). For those players, games after leaving are no better than before joining. Returns to the first franchise cannot be tested this way and run +0.35.

Limitations

  • Survivors only. A revenge game exists only for a player good enough to be employed by a second team and active on the day. The fixed effects remove his level, but not a selection on unobservable in-season form (for example, a player who is healthy on revenge day). That bias would push the estimate up.
  • Opponent-specific scouting cuts both ways. The former team knows his tendencies; he knows their scheme and personnel. The estimate is the net of both, and cannot separate motivation from information.
  • Connected-franchise effects. Both leagues show a placebo bump near the move (NFL +0.46 in the season before joining, from a post-hoc split with an interval that includes zero; NBA +0.14 pooled, with the same decay-with-distance as revenge). An audition effect alone would explain the placebo without inflating revenge games; revenge is contaminated only if a lasting player-by-franchise edge exists that teams select on. The NBA within-pair design (−0.03) covers only players who faced the franchise before joining it, never the first franchise (Placebo tests). The NFL cannot test any of this with useful precision.
  • Precision. The NFL interval runs from +0.03 to +0.68; removing the 10 largest revenge games leaves +0.20 (p=0.191), though the same removal moves any 1,547 right-skewed fantasy games about as much (Robustness), and leaving out 2017-19 gives p=0.093. We cannot tell where in the distribution the effect comes from.
  • Level heterogeneity is fragile. Level subgroups change sign with the way level is measured (Heterogeneity); v02 uses the previous season, which is pre-determined, and treats the result as exploratory.
  • Stat-line games. The weekly NFL file has no row for a game with zero recorded stats, and former-team game counts are built from stat-line games (playoffs included). Snap counts (S12) fix this from 2012 and do not change the estimate, but pre-2012 seasons rely on stat lines.
  • Departure type is coarse. "Left by trade" comes from the nfldata trade ledger, which starts in 2002; earlier departures default to "left another way". There is no NBA trade flag.
  • Coaching and usage. Targets and carries are outcomes here, not controls. If coaches feed a player against his old team, that is counted as part of the revenge effect, which is the right definition for a fantasy manager.
  • Famous-case tables are illustrations. Both famous lists were written with the data in hand (Fantasy calibration, NBA replication); only the objective marquee sets and the regressions are evidence.
  • What a manager knew at kickoff. The stint fixed effect uses the whole season. A prior-games baseline (S11) gives +0.18 with an interval crossing zero, but it compares moved players with everyone and players who changed teams tend to fade in-season. Among players who had changed teams the same kickoff baseline gives +0.39 (p=0.045) (Robustness).
  • NBA data. The archive ends with 2022-23, and that season's file is missing the last few games for every team.

Reproducibility

Run the scripts in order from ebk-revenge-game/scripts (Python 3, pandas, numpy, scipy, matplotlib, pyarrow, openpyxl). Bootstrap and permutation seeds are fixed (20260923). v01 tables and figures are archived in outputs/archive_v01; v02 tables and figures in outputs/archive_v02; the item-by-item change logs are reports/changelog_c1.md, reports/changelog_c2.md and reports/changelog_c3.md. Payback Is a Rounding Error

Across 1,547 NFL games against a former team, the revenge bump comes to about a third of a fantasy point. Home field is worth about the same.
